headline.text: Label notes possible reaction symptoms with alcohol during metronidazole therapy while studies observed no increased effects

reported.text: The label states abdominal cramps, nausea, vomiting, headaches and flushing may occur with alcohol during metronidazole therapy.
In 12 healthy male volunteers, metronidazole with ethanol caused no objective or subjective disulfiram-like effects and did not raise blood acetaldehyde versus placebo.
In 36 emergency patients, metronidazole with ethanol showed no more disulfiram-like effects than ethanol alone.

mechanism.text: Metronidazole with ethanol is thought to block hepatic ALDH, causing acetaldehyde accumulation.

summary.text: The label describes possible reaction symptoms with alcohol during metronidazole therapy, while small volunteer and emergency patient studies observed no increased disulfiram-like effects.

pharmacistQuestions.text: The label and a published study disagree here. Which finding fits my situation better?
Do any of my other medicines or products, like cough syrup or mouthwash, contain alcohol?
Does my dose, or the time between taking Metronidazole and drinking alcohol, change how much this matters?

claims.text: The label states abdominal cramps, nausea, vomiting, headaches, flushing may occur with alcohol during metronidazole therapy.
claims.quote: Abdominal cramps, nausea, vomiting, headaches, and flushing may occur if alcoholic beverages or products containing propylene glycol are consumed during or following metronidazole therapy (see CONTRAINDICATIONS ) .
claims.judgeRationale: Supports: the label quote explicitly warns that these symptoms may occur if alcohol is consumed during metronidazole therapy, matching the claim's co-exposure, symptoms, and may-occur certainty for increases_risk.

claims.text: In 12 healthy male volunteers, metronidazole with ethanol caused no objective or subjective disulfiram-like effects versus placebo.
claims.quote:
Of 12 healthy male volunteers in this double-blind study, one-half received metronidazole for 5 days and the other half received placebo. All volunteers received ethanol 0.4 g/kg at the beginning of the study. Repeated blood samples were taken every 20 minutes for 4 hours, and blood acetaldehyde and ethanol concentrations were determined. Blood pressure, heart rate, and skin temperature were also measured every 20 minutes for objective signs of a possible disulfiram-like reaction. Volunteers also completed a questionnaire focusing on the subjective signs of disulfiram-like reaction.

Metronidazole did not raise blood acetaldehyde or have any objective or subjective adverse effects when used together with ethanol.
claims.judgeRationale: The quote reports a placebo-controlled comparison in 12 healthy male volunteers where metronidazole plus ethanol produced no objective or subjective disulfiram-like effects, matching the bounded no-effect-observed claim.

claims.text: Metronidazole with ethanol is thought to block hepatic ALDH, causing acetaldehyde accumulation.
claims.quote: Metronidazole, an effective antianaerobic agent, has been reported to have aversive properties when ingested with ethanol. This is thought to be due to the blocking of hepatic aldehyde dehydrogenase (ALDH) enzyme followed by the accumulation of acetaldehyde in the blood.
claims.judgeRationale: Supports, because the quote explicitly states the metronidazole-ethanol aversive effect is thought to result from blocking hepatic ALDH and subsequent acetaldehyde accumulation, matching the hedged mechanism claim.

claims.text: In 36 emergency patients, metronidazole with ethanol showed no more disulfiram-like effects than ethanol alone.
claims.quote: A retrospective chart review was performed from December 1, 2010, through December 31, 2020 on emergency department patients with ethanol use confirmed via detectable ethanol concentration who received metronidazole while ethanol was predicted to still be present in the serum. A matched comparator group with the same ethanol concentrations, as well as sex and age, was generated for comparison. The incidence of disulfiram-like reaction symptoms documented in the medical record was compared between groups. P Thirty-six patients were included in the study: 18 in the metronidazole group and 18 in the ethanol concentration matched control group. The mean age in both groups was 46 years. The metronidazole group was 50% male, and the mean ethanol concentration was 0.21 g/dL. The control group was 44.4% male. There was significantly less hypertension in the metronidazole group compared to the control group (16.7% vs 61.1%,  $lt;  0.0001). There were no other significant difference in disulfiram-like effects between the two groups.
claims.judgeRationale: The quote reports a matched comparison of 36 emergency patients (18 receiving metronidazole with ethanol versus 18 with ethanol alone) finding no significantly greater disulfiram-like effects, which supports the no_effect_observed claim.
